result.overall: The judicial review application was dismissed because the Board reasonably concluded that the applicant's unexplained 14-month delay in making a refugee claim indicated a lack of subjective fear of persecution.

themes.name: Delay in making refugee claim
themes.summary: The Board considered the 14-month delay in making the refugee claim as a key factor indicating lack of subjective fear of persecution.

themes.name: Applicant's credibility and explanations
themes.summary: The applicant's explanations for the delay and his credibility were assessed and found unsatisfactory by the Board and the Court.

themes.name: Psychological report relevance
themes.summary: The psychological report showed past symptoms in Mexico but no current issues that would explain the delay in Canada, and was not found to justify the delay.

themes.name: Legal standard on subjective fear and delay
themes.summary: The jurisprudence supports that delay can be relevant to subjective fear but is not determinative unless unexplained; the Board applied this correctly.

issue_map.label: Judicial review application and standard of review

Applicant's arguments against Board's findings on delay and credibility
Legal principles on delay and subjective fear of persecution
Analysis of applicant's explanations and psychological report
Court's conclusion on reasonableness of Board's decision and dismissal of application

arguments.quote: The Board found the applicant not to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, determining that the applicant lacked a subjective fear of persecution.
arguments.claim: The Board found the applicant was not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection because he lacked a subjective fear of persecution.

arguments.quote: To reach its conclusion, the Board focussed on the applicant's long delay in making a refugee claim in Canada.
arguments.claim: The Board focussed on the applicant's long delay in making a refugee claim in Canada.

arguments.quote: Indeed, the applicant arrived in Canada on March 25, 1999, but did not submit a refugee claim until May 2000.
arguments.claim: The applicant arrived in Canada on March 25, 1999, but did not submit a refugee claim until May 2000, a 14 months delay.

arguments.quote: Considering the applicant's claim of fear of imprisonment, torture and death in Mexico, the Board found this 14 months delay to be inexplicable.
arguments.claim: Considering the applicant's claim of fear of imprisonment, torture and death in Mexico, the Board found this 14 months delay to be inexplicable.

arguments.quote: After a thorough analysis of the case law on the relevance of delay in making a refugee claim, the Board stated that such delay may indeed point to a lack of subjective fear of persecution.
arguments.claim: The Board stated that delay in making a refugee claim may point to a lack of subjective fear of persecution.

arguments.quote: The Board stated that the importance one gives to the element of delay depends on the circumstances of each case, the more inexplicable the delay, the greater the probability that subjective fear is absent.
arguments.claim: The importance given to delay depends on the circumstances; the more inexplicable the delay, the greater the probability that subjective fear is absent.

arguments.quote: The Board concluded that the circumstances of this case are such that the element of delay is not only relevant but assumes a decisive role.
arguments.claim: The Board concluded that delay is not only relevant but assumes a decisive role in this case.

arguments.quote: The Board noted that while the applicant was granted admission as a visitor for the first six months and may not have felt a pressing need to make a claim during this time, he was unable to explain his later delays.
arguments.claim: The Board noted the applicant was admitted as a visitor for six months and may not have felt a pressing need to claim then, but could not explain later delays.

arguments.quote: The Board found this delay to be all the more unexplainable given that according to the applicant's Personal Information Form (PIF), he spoke with a lawyer who advised him to make a refugee claim "a few months" after arriving in Canada : "At one point, he said he was focused upon earning money. At another point, he said that the peace and tranquility he found in Canada had lulled his sense of danger.
arguments.claim: The applicant spoke with a lawyer who advised him to make a refugee claim a few months after arriving, but he delayed, giving various explanations such as focusing on earning money and feeling lulled by peace in Canada.

arguments.quote: He had apparently lost all sense of time. Asked what would have happened if his illegal status had been discovered, the claimant had no reply to give. Asked if he had gone into the Internet to find out information on how to make a claim, he replied that he had not.
arguments.claim: The applicant said he lost all sense of time, had no reply about consequences of illegal status discovery, and did not seek information on making a claim online.

arguments.quote: All this is extremely surprising in that the claimant had four years study of law in Mexico and was on the verge of graduating with a degree in law. If any claimant was equipped to inform himself on the Canadian refugee system, this was the claimant. Yet he did nothing."
arguments.claim: The Board found it surprising that the applicant, with four years of law study and near graduation, did not inform himself about the refugee system and did nothing.

arguments.quote: The Board pointed out that the applicant had no mental or personality problems and was in full command of his senses.
arguments.claim: The Board pointed out the applicant had no mental or personality problems and was in full command of his senses.

arguments.quote: The Board concluded that his inaction following his arrival in Canada can be interpreted to mean that he has no fear of serious harm in Mexico.
arguments.claim: The Board concluded the applicant's inaction after arrival can be interpreted as meaning he has no fear of serious harm in Mexico.

arguments.quote: Thus, it rejected the applicant's claim for its lack of subjective basis.
arguments.claim: The Board rejected the applicant's claim for lack of subjective basis due to the delay and inaction.

arguments.quote: The applicant argues that it was irrational for the Board to conclude that the only possible explanation for the applicant not making a refugee claim for 14 months after arrival in Canada was a lack of fear of serious harm in Mexico.
arguments.claim: It was irrational for the Board to conclude that the only possible explanation for the 14-month delay in making a refugee claim was a lack of fear of serious harm in Mexico.

arguments.quote: The applicant submits that, while the applicant's PIF narrative may be imprecise and misleading on the point, he first went to see a lawyer about his options some 8 or 9 months after arriving in Canada (as opposed to "a few months" indicated in his PIF) and as such, this aspect of the delay was much shorter than the Board indicated.
arguments.claim: The delay was shorter than the Board indicated because he first consulted a lawyer 8 or 9 months after arrival, not just a few months as stated in his PIF.

arguments.quote: Furthermore, the applicant agues that the Board totally ignored his explanation as to why he did nothing after consulting the first lawyer; his excuse was that he had no money to finance a refugee claim and was put off by the lawyer that he first met.
arguments.claim: The Board ignored his explanation that he did nothing after consulting the first lawyer because he had no money and was discouraged by that lawyer.

arguments.quote: Furthermore, the applicant argues that Board misconstrued the evidence, especially the psychological report. The applicant argues that while the psychological report found that the applicant was not currently suffering from any psychological problems, it alleged that he had suffered from clinically significant symptoms of depression and anxiety while living in Mexico.
arguments.claim: The Board misconstrued the psychological report, which found no current psychological problems but did find clinically significant depression and anxiety while he lived in Mexico.

arguments.quote: The applicant argues that the Board erred in concluding that all persons fleeing persecution or serious harm are always motivated to make a refugee claim at the first practicable opportunity.
arguments.claim: The Board erred in concluding that all persons fleeing persecution or serious harm are always motivated to make a refugee claim at the first practicable opportunity.

arguments.quote: The applicant's most persuasive argument that delay is a significant factor to be considered in refugee claims but not decisive in itself and cannot be examined in isolation. The applicant submits that the Board did not assess his credibility nor the risk of harm to him in Mexico, and thus erred by basing its decision solely on the delay.
arguments.claim: Delay is a significant factor but not decisive and cannot be examined in isolation; the Board erred by not assessing his credibility or risk of harm and basing its decision solely on delay.

arguments.quote: Regarding the psychological report, the respondent notes that this report makes no findings as to the applicant's delay in claiming refugee status, nor does it reference any symptoms applicable to the applicant after his arrival in Canada that would render him incapable of submitting a refugee claim for 14 months.
arguments.claim: The psychological report does not address the applicant's delay in claiming refugee status or indicate symptoms after arrival that would prevent him from submitting a claim for 14 months.

arguments.quote: Referring to the applicant's affidavit filed in support the respondent argues that even at the time the applicant submitted his refugee claim he was not totally convinced he wanted to stay in Canada; that the impetus for his decision to "commit himself to staying into Canada" was not his fear of persecution in Mexico but rather the initiation of a serious relationship in Canada; had the applicant really feared for his security and his life as alleged, this concern should have taken precedence over other considerations.
arguments.claim: The applicant was not fully convinced to stay in Canada when he submitted his refugee claim; his decision was motivated by a relationship, not fear of persecution.

arguments.quote: Referring to the applicant's affidavit filed in support the respondent argues that even at the time the applicant submitted his refugee claim he was not totally convinced he wanted to stay in Canada; that the impetus for his decision to "commit himself to staying into Canada" was not his fear of persecution in Mexico but rather the initiation of a serious relationship in Canada; had the applicant really feared for his security and his life as alleged, this concern should have taken precedence over other considerations.
arguments.claim: If the applicant truly feared for his security and life, that fear would have outweighed other considerations and prompted an earlier claim.

arguments.quote: Indeed, despite the applicant's alleged fear of imprisonment, torture and death in Mexico, his background (legal training for four years) and his admission that he consulted a lawyer who advised him to make a refugee claim between a few months and 8 months of his arrival in Canada contradicts his assertion.
arguments.claim: The applicant's background and admission of consulting a lawyer who advised him to make a refugee claim between a few months and 8 months after arrival contradict his assertion of fear of imprisonment, torture and death in Mexico.

arguments.quote: The applicant's explanations included that he "was focused on earning money", that the peace and tranquillity in Canada "lulled his sense of danger", that he did "not in fact enter into a serious relationship with anyone until about 18 months after [he] had arrived in Canada and until then [he] did not really feel a strong desire to commit [himself] to staying permanently in Canada". This so-called justification is certainly not persuasive.
arguments.claim: The applicant explained his delay by saying he was focused on earning money, felt lulled by peace and tranquillity in Canada, and did not enter into a serious relationship until about 18 months after arrival, so did not feel a strong desire to stay permanently.

arguments.quote: This so-called justification is certainly not persuasive.
arguments.claim: The Board found the applicant's justification for delay not persuasive.

arguments.quote: Regarding the psychological report, dated August 28, 2002, it is written that the applicant was "not currently suffering from any psychological problems"; an observation also noted by the Board.
arguments.claim: The psychological report dated August 28, 2002, stated the applicant was not currently suffering from any psychological problems, an observation also noted by the Board.

arguments.quote: The report was based on a single interview held on August_22, 2002 and it asserts that he may have been suffering from clinically significant symptoms of depression and anxiety "while living in Mexico".
arguments.claim: The psychological report was based on a single interview and asserted the applicant may have had clinically significant symptoms of depression and anxiety while living in Mexico.

arguments.quote: It does not provide any medical explanation justifying the applicant's inaction during the 14 months.
arguments.claim: The psychological report did not provide any medical explanation justifying the applicant's inaction during the 14 months delay.

arguments.quote: The Board did not accept the applicant's evidence or his explanation to justify the delay and rejected them as unsatisfactory.
arguments.claim: The Board did not accept the applicant's evidence or explanation for the delay and found them unsatisfactory.

holdings.quote: This is an application for judicial review pursuant to section 18.1(3)b) of the Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, with respect to a decision of the Convention Refugee Determination Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (the "Board") dated October 3, 2002, wherein the Board determined that Roberto Pablo Hernandez Espinosa (the "applicant") is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection.
holdings.statement: This is an application for judicial review under section 18.1(3)b) of the Federal Court Act concerning a decision of the Convention Refugee Determination Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board dated October 3, 2002.

holdings.quote: The applicant is a 29-year-old citizen of Mexico who claims a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of his homosexuality.
holdings.statement: The applicant is a 29-year-old citizen of Mexico who claims a well-founded fear of persecution because of his homosexuality.

holdings.quote: He alleges to have suffered from harassment by the Mexican police because of his sexual orientation and that he has been subject to hostility from the family of a woman he has impregnated in Mexico.
holdings.statement: He alleges harassment by the Mexican police due to his sexual orientation and hostility from the family of a woman he impregnated in Mexico.

holdings.quote: It is trite law, as the Board recognized, that in assessing a applicant's subjective fear of persecution, the Board can take into consideration the applicant's behaviour.
holdings.statement: In assessing an applicant's subjective fear of persecution, the Board can consider the applicant's behaviour, including delay in claiming refugee status.

holdings.quote: As the Board states, delay points to a lack of subjective fear of persecution, the reasoning being that someone who was truly fearful would claim refugee status at the first opportunity.
holdings.statement: Delay in claiming refugee status points to a lack of subjective fear of persecution because someone truly fearful would claim refugee status at the first opportunity.

holdings.quote: The Board states correctly that while the delay is generally not a determinative factor in a refugee claim, there are circumstances where the delay can be such that it assumes a decisive role; what is fatal to the applicant's claim is his inability to provide any satisfactory explanation for the delay.
holdings.statement: While delay is generally not determinative in a refugee claim, there are circumstances where delay can assume a decisive role, especially if the applicant cannot provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay.

holdings.quote: This Court accepts that it was not unreasonable for the Board to conclude, based on the evidence before it, that the applicant's inaction following his arrival in Canada demonstrated that he had no fear of serious harm in Mexico and thus "no subjective basis to his claim".
holdings.statement: It was not unreasonable for the Board to conclude that the applicant's inaction after arriving in Canada showed he had no subjective fear of serious harm in Mexico.

holdings.quote: Furthermore, the Board correctly analysed the jurisprudence pertaining to the delays.
holdings.statement: The Board correctly analysed the jurisprudence related to delays in refugee claims.

holdings.quote: There is no doubt that the jurisprudence is clear; the delay of a refugee claim is related to the existence of a subjective fear of persecution, the essential element of a claim.
holdings.statement: The jurisprudence clearly links delay in a refugee claim to the existence of a subjective fear of persecution, which is an essential element of the claim.

holdings.quote: There is no error of law.
holdings.statement: There was no error of law in the Board's decision regarding the delay and subjective fear of persecution.

holdings.quote: For these reasons, I hereby dismiss the application for judicial review.
holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is dismissed.

authorities.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal in Heer v. M.E.I. (13 April 1988) Doc. No. A-474-87 (F.C.A.) recognized that an applicant's delay in claiming refugee status "is an important factor which the Board is entitled to consider in weighing a claim for refugee status".
authorities.authority: The Federal Court of Appeal in Heer v. M.E.I. recognized that an applicant's delay in claiming refugee status is an important factor the Board can consider in weighing a refugee claim.
